samples.text: In floating‑point arithmetic the numbers are stored with a finite number of bits, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. Because rounding can change the magnitude of the intermediate result, \((a+b)+c\) may be rounded after the first addition and then again after the second, while \(a+(b+c)\) rounds only after the second addition. The two possible rounding errors are generally different, so the final stored values can differ, showing that floating‑point addition is not associative.

samples.text: In floating‑point arithmetic numbers are stored with a finite number of bits, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. Because rounding can alter the magnitude of an intermediate result, computing \((a+b)+c\) (which rounds after the first addition) can yield a different value than computing \(a+(b+c)\) (which rounds after the second addition). Consequently, the limited precision and mandatory rounding steps break the mathematical associativity property for floating‑point addition.
